headline: Conimicut ledge holds after dark, bluefish tear up Greenwich Bay bunker
subhead: Bass have gone nocturnal on the bay's warm water, but the blues won't let you feel bad about it.
body_markdown:
Ran into Dominic down at the Sabin Point launch Tuesday morning, hauling his kayak up the ramp looking like he hadn't slept — because he hadn't. Told me he anchored up off Nyatt Point at eleven the night before and didn't touch bottom with the plug until almost 1 a.m. when the bass finally showed. That's where we're at now on the bay. It's July, the water's sitting in the mid-70s off Conimicut and Rocky Point, and the stripers have punched out on the daytime program almost entirely. If you want them, you're fishing the dark.

We flagged this last week — said the pattern would hold with no big thermal shift coming, and that's exactly what happened. The bay didn't cool, didn't get a flush of fresh water, nothing changed the equation. Bass are stacked deep off the drop at Conimicut Point, sitting on that hard bottom in 25 to 35 feet, and they're not coming up to feed until the sun's been down an hour or two. Guys working the outgoing tide after 10 p.m. with eels — live or the SP Minnow in black — are getting into fish in the mid-20s to low 30-inch class right off the light. Same story working the west side of Prudence, along that deep edge that runs off Sandy Point down toward the south end. Slow-trolled bunker chunks on a three-way rig, fished right on the bottom during the last two hours of the ebb, has been the more consistent producer than anything thrown on the surface.

Daytime, if you insist on fishing sunlight, your better play is bouncing bucktails — half-ounce to an ounce, white or chartreuse — along the rocky ledges off Rocky Point and out toward the Hope Island reef structure. You'll pick at fish, not load the boat, but there's enough there to keep it honest, especially right on the tide change when the current goes slack for twenty minutes and everything that's been holding tight to structure fans out to feed.

Bluefish are the story you can actually fish in daylight right now, and they're making up for the bass going quiet. Greenwich Bay has had bunker pushed up tight against the shoreline all week, and the blues have been running through them hard off Warwick Neck and along the flats inside Rocky Point. If you see the bunker nervous on the surface — and this week you will, they've been balled up thick off the Cove and out toward Chepiwanoxet — throw a Hopkins or a Deadly Dick, silver, and you don't need to work it much. Blues in the 3 to 6 pound range, some better, and they'll cut a light leader clean if you're not running at least 30-pound fluorocarbon up top. This bluefish push is part of the same bunker migration that's been running the whole coast, and there's no sign it's slowing down here — the schools keep refreshing every few days.

Fluke have moved into their typical mid-summer pattern, meaning the shallow flats are stuffed with shorts and the keepers have slid into deeper, cooler water. Best fish this week have come from the channel edge off Nayatt Point and down around the mouth of the Providence River near the Fields Point range markers, working 4-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, drifted slow on the last of the incoming when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping. Twenty-eight to 35 feet is where the better grade has been sitting. Greenwich Bay itself is loaded with shorts right now — fun for kids and a fast rod, but you're throwing most of them back.

Scup fishing stays the reliable summer program it always is. The reefs off Prudence Island and the rock piles around Ohio Ledge are stacked, and if you want a box of fish for the table there's no easier program in the bay — squid strips or clam on a hi-lo rig, bounced bottom in 15 to 25 feet, any tide stage. Black sea bass mixed in on the same structure, though you're culling a lot of shorts to find keepers this deep into the season.

No sign of the herring run mattering anymore this time of year — that's a spring story, Buckeye Brook emptied out back in May and the bass that rode that bait into the upper bay have long since scattered onto their summer program. But it's worth remembering because it tells you something about how these fish move: they follow the food, and right now the food that matters is bunker in the mid-bay and whatever bottom bait's holding on the ledges.

Looking ahead, I don't see anything changing this pattern through the weekend. Wind's been light, no fronts pushing through, water's stable and warm. If I had one night to fish, I'd be back at Conimicut on the last two hours of the outgoing, eeling the drop after dark. If I had one afternoon, I'd run Greenwich Bay looking for bunker getting nervous on top — that bite can turn on in five minutes and be over in twenty, so keep the reel ready and don't wander far from the bay-side shoreline where the schools have been holding tightest.
